claims.text: A multimodal machine-learning framework can identify optimal thermomechanical processing routes for structural HEAs.
Machine-learning-guided thermomechanical processing can generate engineered gradient dual-phase microstructures in HEAs.
The targeted microstructure has a spatial variation in phase distribution.
The targeted dual-phase microstructure may combine soft FCC and hard BCC phases with tailored interfaces.
Engineered phase gradients and interfaces enhance load sharing.
Engineered phase gradients and interfaces improve stress distribution.
Optimized phase interactions can decouple conventional mechanical-property trade-offs.
ML-optimized processing is expected to increase strength relative to conventional processing.
ML-optimized processing is expected to increase ductility relative to conventional processing.
ML-optimized processing is expected to increase Young's modulus relative to conventional processing.
ML-optimized processing is expected to increase fracture resistance relative to conventional processing.
The anticipated improvements should hold within the processing and composition domain represented by the ML training data.
The method may be ineffective when the input data are sparse.
The method may be ineffective for alloy compositions that promote unstable phase distributions.
The method may not generalize to extreme temperatures or strain rates outside the validated parameter space.
Conventionally processed HEAs typically exhibit trade-offs between strength and ductility, modulus, or fracture resistance.
Prior trends involving optimized eutectic and vermicular microstructures support the predicted direction of improvement.
The magnitude of improvement is alloy-dependent and sensitive to processing precision.
The success of the approach depends on the quality and representativeness of the experimental data supplied to the ML framework.
